Euclidean geometry is a mathematical system attributed to Alexandrian Greek mathematician Euclid, which he described in his textbook: the Elements. Euclid's method consists in assuming a small set of intuitively appealing axioms, and deducing many other propositions from these.

The fundamental concepts include points, lines, planes, and angles. According to the first axiom, a straight line segment can be drawn joining any two points. This simple foundation allows for the construction of complex geometric shapes and the derivation of the Pythagorean theorem.

In modern times, Euclidean geometry remains the basis for architectural design and classical physics, providing the necessary framework for understanding the space we inhabit.

title: The Social Contract: Rights and Obligations

versions.content: The social contract is a theory or model that originated during the Age of Enlightenment and usually concerns the legitimacy of the authority of the state over the individual. It posits that individuals have consented, either explicitly or tacitly, to surrender some of their freedoms to a ruler in exchange for protection of their remaining rights.

The social contract is a theory or model that originated during the Age of Enlightenment and usually concerns the legitimacy of the authority of the state over the individual. It posits that individuals have consented, either explicitly or tacitly, to surrender some of their freedoms to a ruler in exchange for protection of their remaining rights.

Thomas Hobbes, John Locke, and Jean-Jacques Rousseau are the most famous philosophers associated with this concept. While Hobbes argued for absolute sovereignty to avoid 'the war of all against all', Locke emphasized that the government's power is limited and based on the consent of the governed.

This philosophical framework continues to influence modern democratic systems and the ongoing debate regarding the balance between national security and personal privacy.

Quantum mechanics is a fundamental theory in physics that provides a description of the physical properties of nature at the scale of atoms and subatomic particles. It is the foundation of all quantum physics including quantum chemistry and quantum field theory.

Quantum mechanics is a fundamental theory in physics that provides a description of the physical properties of nature at the scale of atoms and subatomic particles. It is the foundation of all quantum physics including quantum chemistry and quantum field theory.

One of the most striking features of this theory is wave-particle duality, which states that every particle or quantum entity may be described as either a particle or a wave. This leads to the Uncertainty Principle, formulated by Werner Heisenberg, asserting that the position and velocity of an object cannot both be measured exactly at the same time.

These concepts challenge our classical intuition but have led to the development of vital technologies, such as transistors, lasers, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

For centuries, the study of primes was considered a branch of pure mathematics with little practical application.

Everything changed with the advent of the digital age and the development of public-key cryptography. The RSA algorithm, named after Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman, relies on the practical difficulty of factoring the product of two large prime numbers. While multiplying two large primes is computationally simple, reversing the process—factoring the resulting giant number—is nearly impossible with current technology.

In software engineering, a design pattern is a general, reusable solution to a commonly occurring problem within a given context in software design. It is not a finished design that can be transformed directly into source or machine code.

The 'Gang of Four' patterns are generally divided into three categories: Creational, Structural, and Behavioral. For instance, the Singleton pattern ensures a class has only one instance, while the Factory pattern deals with the problem of creating objects without specifying the exact class of object that will be created.

Behavioral patterns, such as the Observer pattern, define how objects communicate. This is particularly useful in JavaFX, where a UI component might need to 'observe' changes in a data model and update itself automatically.

General relativity is the geometric theory of gravitation published by Albert Einstein in 1915. It remains the current description of gravitation in modern physics, generalizing special relativity and Newton's law of universal gravitation to provide a unified description of gravity as a geometric property of space and time, or spacetime.

According to Einstein, massive objects cause a curvature in spacetime, which is experienced as gravity. Rather than being an invisible force pulling objects toward each other, gravity is the result of objects following the shortest path (geodesics) through a curved four-dimensional fabric. As Wheeler famously put it: 'Spacetime tells matter how to move; matter tells spacetime how to curve.'

The predictions of general relativity, such as the bending of light around massive stars and the existence of black holes, have been confirmed by a century of observational data. Most recently, the detection of gravitational waves—ripples in the fabric of spacetime caused by massive cosmic collisions—has opened a new window into observing the universe.

Existentialism is a philosophical inquiry that explores the nature of the human condition, focusing on the experience of the individual as a self-determining agent. It suggests that individuals are entirely free and, therefore, responsible for what they make of themselves. With this responsibility comes a profound sense of angst or dread, as there is no pre-determined 'essence' to guide human life.

Existentialism is a philosophical inquiry that explores the nature of the human condition, focusing on the experience of the individual as a self-determining agent. It suggests that individuals are entirely free and, therefore, responsible for what they make of themselves. With this responsibility comes a profound sense of angst or dread, as there is no pre-determined 'essence' to guide human life.

The famous dictum 'existence precedes essence', coined by Jean-Paul Sartre, encapsulates this movement. It argues that humans first exist, encounter themselves, surge up in the world, and define themselves afterwards. Unlike a tool, such as a paperknife, which is designed with a specific purpose in mind, a human being begins as nothing and becomes what they choose to be through their actions.

This emphasis on radical freedom and personal authenticity has deeply influenced literature, psychology, and theology. Philosophers like Albert Camus added the layer of 'The Absurd', suggesting that while humans naturally search for inherent meaning in life, the universe remains indifferently silent, forcing the individual to create their own meaning.

Game theory is the study of mathematical models of strategic interaction among rational decision-makers. Originally developed to address zero-sum games, in which one person's gains result in losses for the other participants, it has expanded to include a wide range of behavioral relations and is now an umbrella term for the science of logical decision-making.

A central concept in game theory is the Nash Equilibrium, named after John Nash. It describes a situation where no player can benefit by changing their strategy while the other players keep theirs unchanged. A classic example is the 'Prisoner's Dilemma,' which illustrates why two completely rational individuals might not cooperate, even if it appears that it is in their best interests to do so.

In modern economics, game theory is used to understand the behavior of firms in oligopolies, the outcomes of auctions, and the dynamics of international trade negotiations. It provides a rigorous framework for predicting how individuals and organizations will behave when their success depends on the choices of others.

Cognitive dissonance is a theory in social psychology proposed by Leon Festinger in 1957. it refers to the mental discomfort experienced by a person who holds two or more contradictory beliefs, ideas, or values. This discomfort is triggered by a situation in which a person's belief clashes with new evidence or with the person's behavior.

To reduce this tension, individuals tend to change either their behavior or their belief to restore consistency. A classic example is smoking: a smoker who knows that the habit is harmful (knowledge) but continues to smoke (behavior) may rationalize their action by saying 'smoking helps me relax' or 'I only smoke light cigarettes.'

This mechanism of self-justification is central to human psychology, influencing everything from consumer choices to political affiliations and social relationships.
